webpage.text:
On the Dylan Thomas trail in Laugharne, Camrthenshire, Wales

Dylan Thomas once famously described Laugharne as the “strangest town in Wales”.

Much has changed since the Welsh poet first visited the Carmarthernshire town in 1934, but the description remains apt.

Laugharne is also arguably one of the most welcoming and beautiful places in the country – a “beguiling island of a town”, in Dylan’s words.

In the 60 years since the poet died in New York after falling ill there at his 39th birthday party, the remote Welsh town has become a Mecca for fans from across the world. 

Thousands are expected to make their pilgrimage there in 2014, which marks the centenary of his birth.

His presence pervades the town – from the whitewashed boathouse overlooking his “heron priested shore”, to lines from Under Milk Wood decorating the wooden shelter beside the “fishingboat-bobbing sea”.

My wife Claire and I stayed at his favourite drinking hole, Brown’s Hotel, from where he would stumble along the dark path back to the boathouse where he wrote many of his most famous works.

The bar has been open to the public for years, but it only recently became a hotel again for the first time since the 1950s after a major refurbishment.

The interior is heavily and stylishly influenced by the look of the day, with exposed beams, classy retro furniture and period features. All, of course, seamlessly mixed with modern essentials like wifi and HDTVs.

Back to the town, and The Boathouse itself has become a museum to the life and times of Dylan.

It features memorabilia and some of the original furniture from his time living there with wife Caitlin, and is close to the small writing shed where he wrote famous works including Do Not Go Gentle and Under Milk Wood.

It overlooks the tranquil Tâf Estuary, home to all kinds of wildlife and offering stunning views immortalised in his Poem in October.

Devotees can follow the two-mile walk to St John’s Hill described in Poem in October, which marked the writer’s “thirtieth year to heaven”.

If, like him, you’re visiting on your own birthday (you’ll need ID to prove it!) there’s a range of treats you can pick up along the way – including a free pint in Brown’s, a bag of chips in the Castle View Takeaway and Restaurant, and a coffee and Welsh Cake at Café Culture.

Locals in no way appear to resent the fact that their town has become so closely associated with the poet. But what they will tell you – again and again – is that there’s more to Laugharne than Dylan Thomas.

We were to discover this within minutes of arriving. What better way to follow in Dylan’s footsteps, we thought, than a night on the town. Our first stop was Laugharne Rugby Club, where we were greeted by landlord Phil Davies – one of the town’s many colourful characters.

It was Phil who first told us some of the unique history of Laugharne, although as the night went on and the beer flowed we were to hear at least 15 different versions.


Laugharne is among the last surviving medieval corporations in the UK, dating back to 1297 when it was granted the status by Royal Charter.

It has a court made up of a portreeve, the aldermen and a body of burgesses. Customs associated with the corporation include “beating the bounds”, which happens on Whit Monday every three years.

This particular custom sees townsfolk – and an increasing number of tourists – embark on a riotous drink-fuelled trek around the boundaries of the township, stomping though woodland, fields and even people’s living rooms.

At various historical landmarks along the trail, a victim is selected to name the place. If they cannot answer they are hoisted upside down and ceremonially beaten three times on the rear.

We unknowingly arrived in the town on a major night in the Laugharne calendar – Big Court Night.This is held on the first Monday after Michaelmas, when the town’s new portreeve – essentially a kind of mayor – is sworn in. 

A new jury is also called from the town burgesses (no women allowed), who are all expected to be present to answer their names at the rollcall. Only long-term residents qualify as burgesses.

In scenes vaguely reminiscent of the Wicker Man, as part of the swearing-in process the new portreeve is draped in a gold chain of cockles and hoisted aloft on a wooden chair, which is then ceremoniously carried three times around the town hall.

Then, in true Dylan Thomas style, it’s off to the pub – where the new portreeve is obliged to buy every burgess a pint. 

On the following Sunday comes an event that will outrage feminists. The portreeve holds a civic breakfast to which only men are invited – and there they are waited on hand and foot by the women of the town.

For another look at history you can visit the Tin Shed Experience, an impressive 1940s museum opened by local men Andrew Isaacs and Seimon Pugh-Jones. An extra perk of visiting Laugharne on your birthday is free entry to this museum.

Nearby you can pay your respects to Dylan at his final resting place, St Martin’s Church.

A modest white wooden cross marks his grave. His beloved Caitlin – with whom he shared a famously tempestuous relationship – is buried in the same plot and her name appears on the reverse side of the cross.

From there it’s another short walk through the town to Laugharne Castle, where Dylan would write in the garden summerhouse.

Inside is a small exhibition detailing the works of another writer who made Laugharne his home – the author Richard Hughes, who first introduced Dylan to the town.

Hughes and his family lived in another of Laugharne’s landmarks, the colourful Castle House. The castle’s ruins offer panoramic views of the estuary and, on a clear day, across to the Gower Peninsula.

In Dylan’s day there were far more pubs, but many have sadly closed in recent years. If there’s one criticism it’s the shortage of quality places to eat – which makes a visit to the nearby Corran Resort & Spa essential ( thecorran.com ). Here we enjoyed a massage in the spa (I’m not sure Dylan would have approved) followed by a cracking meal and lots of wine in the Corran’s excellent restaurant (he’d surely have been all for that).

Laugharne will be at the centre of next year’s centenary celebrations. But even if you’re not a fan, you’ll enjoy immersing yourself in what he described as the “legendary lazy little black-magical bedlam by the sea”.


TRAVEL FILE

Hot tip

Grab a drink at The Three Mariners pub. Next door to Brown’s Hotel ( brownshotel.com ) it does a fab breakfast and its cute outside area gives you a gorgeous view of the stars in the evening. 

Visit

Laugharne Castle. Amazing views over the bay, and lots of (pre-Dylan) history to mix things up a bit.
cadw.wales.gov.uk

Don't Miss

The boathouse. It’s got all you need to know about Dylan Thomas’s colourful life, and wonderful poetry.
www.dylanthomasboathouse.com

Getting There

It really is best to drive.You can hire from Europcar ( europcar.co.uk ) from £19 per day based on a seven-day hire. But the First Cymru bus 222 runs from Carmarthen to Laugharne for £3, eight times a day.

More Info

webpage.text:
Laugharne

Even if you know or care nothing about Dylan Thomas, you’ll want to visit Laugharne in Wales, an enchanting small town. It was part of our tour through Swansea and Carmarthenshire on the Dylan Thomas Trail.

In this article, discover some of the best things to do in Laugharne, with its wide skies and seascapes that inspired the poet. Read my other articles about our visit to Swansea where the poet grew up, and the Dylan Thomas birthplace, his family home in Swansea.


This article may contain affiliate links that provide commission on purchases you make at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.


Laugharne and Dylan Thomas

I like to imagine the 19 year old aspiring poet, Dylan Thomas arriving at Laugharne on the ferry. He would be taking in the wide open skies of the Taf estuary. He’d see small boats stranded in the marshy channels and the stark, stone towers of the ruined castle.


Later he wrote that it was the sort of place where people like him ” just came, one day, for the day, and never left; got off the bus, and forgot to get on again.” Laugharne in Carmarthenshire is one of the places most connected to Dylan Thomas.

He lived for the last 4 years of his life in The Boathouse overlooking the estuary. This locale inspired him to write some of his greatest poetry.


> You may also enjoy: A scenic walk in the South Wales valleys & the Valleys Walking Festival


Brown’s Hotel Laugharne – Dylan Thomas’s favourite pub

We’d already spent Saturday in Swansea, discovering the city that Dylan knew as a young man. Later we drove to Laugharne where we were booked into Brown’s Hotel.

As we pulled up, the evening sun lit up the front of the Georgian pub. This favourite drinking haunt of Dylan Thomas has now been renovated as a bar and boutique hotel.


When he lived here, Dylan’s routine was to sit in the window seat of Brown’s in the morning, studying the papers. Or, he would drop in to see his parents Jack and Florence who lived at The Pelican opposite.

Later it was home to the Boathouse for lunch and working in the writing shed in the afternoon. Usually he returned to Brown’s in the evening with his wife Caitlin for a few more beers.


> You may also enjoy: 12 Breathtaking things to do in North East Wales


Each room individually designed

Our room was The Laques, named after a part of Laugharne that you can see from the bedroom window where Flemish weavers once settled. Note: the hotel has been renovated and the decor updated since we visited.


Each of the 14 rooms at Brown’s Hotel is individually designed in rich colours of aubergine, olive and grey. They feature tactile velvets and soft woollens in the upholstery and bed throws.

All the bedrooms have a natural Welsh wool mattress and are well equipped with digital radios, pod coffee machines and mini fridge. In the bathrooms are eco friendly Anyah toiletries and specially commissioned wall art giving each room its own personality.


The bathrooms are stylish and modern with a nod to the retro, vintage feel that carries through the room decor. In addition to the famous bar, the hotel now has Dexter’s steak house and grill.

Dexter’s showcases dry aged beef from the Dexter breed of cattle farmed locally at Llywn Farm. For those who don’t eat red meat there are also some chicken and fish options available.

> Brown’s Hotel, King Street, Laugharne, Carmarthenshire.


The Taf estuary – views that inspired Dylan Thomas

Taking advantage of the evening sunshine, we followed signs along the lane towards The Boathouse. This is where Dylan Thomas lived with his family. From the lane above the house, I caught the beautiful views over the Taf estuary, where the water was gently rippling and glittering in the evening light.

> Read about 15 fun things to do in Carmarthenshire, Wales


The tide was out with the sandbanks exposed at low tide and some wading seabirds picking their way gingerly through the shallows. This was the view that inspired Dylan to write his Poem in October about his walk from here to St John’s Hill where the wood overlooks the town.

> It was my thirtieth year to heaven
> 
> Woke to my hearing from harbour and neighbour wood
> 
> And the mussel pooled and the heron Priested shore
> 
> The morning beckon
> 
> With water praying and call of seagull and rook
> 
> And the knock of sailing boats on the net webbed wall


Follow the Dylan Thomas birthday walk

> You can follow the route Dylan described in his Poem in October, on the Dylan Thomas Birthday walk. There are benches and signs along the way so that you can read each line or verse at the place it was written. Visit the Dylan Thomas Birthday Walk Website with all the information you need. There’s also an App of the Dylan Thomas Birthday Walk for iPhone and Android.


The Dylan Thomas Grave in Laugharne

On Sunday morning we enjoyed a good cooked breakfast in the bar at Brown’s Hotel. We were surrounded by memorabilia and mementos of Dylan Thomas.

Then we walked up the main street towards St Martin’s church, through the main churchyard gate and over the little footbridge across the lane. Here we found the plain white cross of Dylan and Caitlin Thomas standing out among the grey gravestones.


In the church there is also a replica of the stone memorial in Poet’s Corner, Westminster Abbey, with Dylan’s lines from the poem Fern Hill “Time held me green and dying, though I sang in my chains like the sea”.

Dylan Thomas died in 1953 aged only 39, while on a poetry reading tour in New York. The cause of his untimely death has never been fully explained but was probably a combination of pneumonia, morphine overdose and heavy drinking. Caitlin Thomas was buried with him in the same grave, after her death in 1994.

Dylan’s father, Jack had died only the year before Dylan himself and Dylan wrote one of his most popular and moving poems Do not go gentle into that good night about his father’s illness.

> Do not go gentle into that good night
> 
> Old age should burn and rave at close of day
> 
> Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

From the peaceful graveyard, we continued up the leafy lane beside the church, fringed by cow parsley and pink campion, taking a shortcut to The Boathouse.


The Boathouse Laugharne – home of Dylan Thomas

In 1938 Dylan and Caitlin visited their friends the writers Richard and Frances Hughes at Castle House in Laugharne and decided to find their own place nearby. The couple moved into a tiny fisherman’s cottage and then into a grander house at SeaView where they lived until 1940 until the war years intervened and they moved to London.

In 1949, The Boathouse which Dylan described as “my sea shaken house on a breakneck of rocks”, was bought for Dylan by his friend and patron, Margaret Taylor and he lived there with Caitlin and the children until his death in 1953.


Striking views across the estuary

Walking down the steps to the whitewashed house, the views across the Taf estuary were striking, not only from all the rooms, but from the balcony running around the house and the terrace at the back where there was originally a landing stage for the coal boats.


Under the roof was the main bedroom which is now an exhibition space with mementoes and information about Dylan’s life. Beyond the small shop was a parlour furnished as it would have been by Dylan and Caitlin and kept for ‘best’ as was the custom. I spotted the desk that had belonged to Dylan’s father and had come from his childhood home at 5 Cwmdonkin Park, since Geoff Haden had told me how he really wanted it back!


Downstairs where the family would have gathered was now a tea room but we were able to sit on the terrace in the sunshine with fabulous views over the estuary where I had a chat with artist in residence, Cheryl Beer, who was playing her ukulele and making up poems with some of the children visiting.

Cheryl had noticed the strips of paper in the writing shed like shopping lists of words, and was asking people to write a line of poetry or prose on a strip of paper, for her artwork. Having read some of the passionate, tender and angry love letters between Dylan and Caitlin, she also was planning to write a song that told the story from Caitlin’s point of view, “as a woman who was often being apologised to”

> You may also enjoy: Exploring the food in North East Wales


The Dylan Thomas writing shed

After visiting The Boathouse we walked back along the path to Dylan’s writing shed which the staff kindly opened for me to take photos, although you can normally only peer through the window. Inside Dylan’s writing desk was set out as if he had just left, with cigarette stubs, strips of words hanging up and that inspiring view right across the estuary.


The first poem he wrote there was Over Sir John’s Hill, in which he describes the birds stalking their prey and bringing death in the midst of this beauty.

> Over Sir John’s hill
> 
> The hawk on fire hangs still
> 
> In a hoisted cloud, at drop of dusk, he pulls to his claws
> 
> And gallows, up the rays of his eyes the small birds of the bay

This is also where Dylan wrote his most famous play for voices, Under Milkwood, inspired in part by the people of Laugharne. Dylan described his work in a letter as “a play, an impression for voices, an entertainment out of the darkness, of the town I live in .. (so that) you come to know the town as an inhabitant of it.. utterly familiar with the places and the people.”


From the writing shed we dropped down a path to the level of the estuary where we walked back along the paved causeway with the marshland ahead of us until Laugharne castle came into view.

> The Dylan Thomas Boathouse, Dylan’s Walk, Laugharne, Carmarthenshire, SA33 4SD


Laugharne castle, Brown as owls

Our final stop of the day was the ruined Laugharne castle which overlooks the marsh and the estuary. The castle was built in the 13th century, probably on top of an earlier Norman castle and it came under siege in the English Civil War and was partly dismantled.


When Dylan first came to Laugharne, the castle and its grounds were in the gardens of Castle House next door, owned by writers Richard and Frances Hughes. Laugharne Castle was described by Dylan in his Poem in October.

> Pale rain over the dwindling harbour
> 
> And over the sea wet church the size of a snail
> 
> With its horns through mist and the castle
> 
> Brown as owls
> 
> But all the gardens
> 
> Of spring and summer were blooming in the tall tales
> 
> Beyond the border and under the lark full cloud.

Dylan was allowed the use of the gazebo in the garden which overlooks the estuary and it was here that he wrote the short stories Portrait of the artist as a Young Dog. A nice touch is that there is a writing desk and old typewriter within the gazebo to recreate how it would have looked when Dylan wrote there.


The castle is now open to the public, although it’s really just a picturesque shell of the castle that the Welsh Lords used to dominate the estuary and port at Laugharne before it silted up. You can climb the tower for views over the estuary, and there’s a Victorian Rose garden which is a pleasant place to sit on a summer afternoon.


> Laugharne Castle is run by CADW and is open April-October 10am-5pm Adults £5.00


Plan your visit to Laugharne

Whether you are a Dylan Thomas fan or not, Laugharne is an enchanting place to visit, for the views of the estuary, the walks up to St John’s Hill, for the Brown as Owls castle, and of course for the fascinating Dylan Thomas connections. Follow where Dylan walked, drink where he drank and be inspired by the beauty of the place and the poetry. In a place like this we might all have a literary masterpiece in us!

River Taf

River in West Wales
Not to be confused with River Taff.


River Taf


Physical characteristics
Length   56 km (35 mi)

The River Taf (Welsh: Afon Taf) is a river in West Wales. It rises in the Preseli Hills, Pembrokeshire, and continues through Carmarthenshire to Laugharne. It is one of the three rivers to enter the sea on the east side of Carmarthen Bay. The other two are the River Gwendraeth and River Tywi.


Course

The River Taf is about 35 miles (56 km) from Crymych to Ginst Point, of which about 9 miles (14 km) is tidal.[1]

Water drains from high ground above the village of Crymych in Pembrokeshire, and at one time flowed at ground level across the main Cardigan–Tenby road (A478) before falling to the level of the Whitland and Cardigan Railway station Crymmych Arms (Great Western Railway) where on the UK Ordnance Survey map of 1866 it is shown as the source of the Taf. The stream fulfills its description "Crymych" (in Welsh "crooked stream") by turning through almost a right angle along the floor of the valley. The stream is mentioned—with various spellings—in records since 1468 and provided both the village and its hostelry with an identity. Modern maps show the source to be 650 feet (200 m) altitude at the foot of Frenni Fawr, close to the defunct railway.[2]

From Crymych the Taf, augmented by numerous minor tributaries, flows ESE to Llanfyrnach; SW through Glandwr, Llanglydwen, Login and Llanfallteg after which it becomes the county boundary between Pembrokeshire and Carmarthenshire, passing several times beneath railway lines. It is joined by the right bank tributary Afon Marlais, and turns east into Carmarthenshire, then runs beneath the A40 road to Whitland; east to St Clears, south to its broad estuary.[2]

Wikimedia Commons has media related to River Taf.


References

 1. ↑ The Journal of Conchology 1979 p 7 "CARMARTHEN BAY. Three large estuaries, the Gwendraeth, Afon Tywi and Afon Taf enter the sea on the east side of Carmarthen Bay and these rivers contribute to deposits of muddy shores.
 2. 1 2 "Ordnance Survey". Retrieved 12 June 2020.

Visiting the Dylan Thomas Boathouse

Last Updated on December 2, 2018 by

I had an incredible experience while we were holidaying this week at Bluestone in Wales. We were heading off to go on a steam train somewhere in the Welsh countryside, but we got horribly lost and it soon became apparent that we’d miss the train. Instead of getting stressed out, I told Hubs to keep driving and see where the road took us. At the next junction there was a sign pointing to “Dylan Thomas Boathouse” so I suggested we follow it.

The road weaved and climbed though the Welsh landscape, wending down through Laugharne and towards the wonderful Taf estuary. We parked at the back of a bakery and walked down the coastal path towards the house, we found his writing shed at the top, almost as he’d left it, the curtains open to afford a view of the sea and the coastline from his writing desk. It made me want a writing space half as special as that. A girl can dream.


We followed the path down some more, leaning over the wall we could see the clean slate roof of his home near the shore of the estuary. We walked down the wooden steps and through his garden, shells littered the flower beds and an old shirt and pair of long johns hung jauntily on the washing line. It felt very intimate and quite special.


Opening his front door we were met with a hubbub of chatter, the home felt warm and welcoming. We were damp from the rain and the small boy was hungry, so we walked down the steep staircase to the bottom and found an old parlour of sorts, we bustled in and found a table in the corner.


A wonderful lady called Cheryl Beer (an award winning singer, song writer and musician) came over for a chat with the boy. She showed him some of her great selection of musical instruments and they were soon playing a variety of drums together, whilst I played with a singing bowl. Together we made some lovely music and it felt very, very special. The house felt almost spiritual and I can’t help but feel that something had drawn us there, especially when we were told that it was the very first International Dylan Thomas Day (on 14th May 2015).


We had tea and cake (both excellent), popped to the gift shop and then lazily walked back up the path to our car. It was an intensely wonderful experience, on the way home we stopped to pay our respects at the grave of the great man at St Martins Church in Laugharne. His grave marked by a simple wooden cross and at its base the ground is scattered with seashells and pennies left by visitors.


In the garden of the boathouse there is a bench with the words “The funny thing is, I find myself going back again and again”; and do you know what, I think I will.

You can find out more about Dylan Thomas boathouse on the website, if you’re in the area I urge you to visit.

webpage.text:
Beautiful Welsh town described as 'beguiling island' by very famous fan

Nestled along the stunning coastline of Wales, this picturesque town was once the home of the famous Welsh poet Dylan Thomas, and its surroundings often inspired his work

This beautiful town sits on the coast of Carmarthenshire in Wales, along the estuary of the River Taf, creating the feel of its very own little island.

Spanning across two decades, the famous poet Dylan Thomas lived in Laugharne and was charmed by its loveliness from the day he visited and fell in love with it in 1934. The Welsh poet has written in spots all across the town, helping to inspire some of his best work.

Pieces of his life are scattered across Laugharne, making it the perfect getaway for those looking to immerse themselves in literature and tales of the past. Many of his homes still stand, acting as signposts of his life and work, including Castle House on Market Street.

This building marks the beginning of his love affair with the Welsh town and that with his partner, Caitlin McNamara, as this home was where they first met. It was a friend and writer, Richard Hughes, who lived in the house, and Thomas would frequently visit, using the grounds as a spot to write, with views of the waterfront.

Eros at number 2 Gosport Street was also his home, for around six months, in what was a cosy fisherman's cottage for the couple. It was here that he wrote a letter addressed to his American publisher, revealing his thoughts on Laugharne.

He describes it as "a very odd town”. He wrote: "A good place, undiscovered by painters… because the sea is mostly mud and nobody knows when the water will come in or go out or where it comes from anyway.”

The poet also famously described the town as “a timeless, mild, beguiling island of a town”. And yet, he couldn't quite keep himself away from it.

The most famed spot belonging to the writer is the rightfully named Dylan Thomas Boathouse, which now acts as a museum to the writer's life. In 1949, Thomas and his wife moved into the boathouse, rent-free thanks to a kind benefactor who was a long-time fan of his work. Here, it seems he found a lot of solitude and peace and a newfound admiration for the little town.

In a letter to Margaret Taylor, who lent him the house, he detailed his love for their new home upon the water. He wrote: "For this place I love and where I want to work… this is it: the place, the house, the workroom, the time.

"All I shall write in this water and tree room on the cliff, every word will be my thanks to you. You have given me a life. And now I am going to live it."

Now, those paying a visit to the area can see the boathouse in all of its glory, perched along the water. It acts as a museum, shop and tearoom with writings of his in the shed and heaps of paraphernalia, along with the view that inspired his poetry.

Many fans of his work and keen adventurers take part in the Dylan Thomas birthday walk, set up in his memory by a local farmer, that takes the same walk he carried out on his 30th birthday. It was this walk that inspired the works of Poem In October, visitors can now walk in the very footsteps that led to him putting these famed words to paper.

jsonld.articleBody: This beautiful town sits on the coast of  Carmarthenshire  in Wales, along the estuary of the River Taf, creating the feel of its very own little island. Spanning across two decades, the famous poet  Dylan Thomas  lived in Laugharne and was charmed by its loveliness from the day he visited and fell in love with it in 1934. The Welsh poet has written in spots all across the town, helping to inspire some of his best work. Pieces of his life are scattered across Laugharne, making it the perfect getaway for those looking to immerse themselves in literature and tales of the past. Many of his homes still stand, acting as signposts of his life and work, including Castle House on Market Street. This building marks the beginning of his love affair with the Welsh town and that with his partner, Caitlin McNamara, as this home was where they first met. It was a friend and writer, Richard Hughes, who lived in the house, and Thomas would frequently visit, using the grounds as a spot to write, with views of the waterfront. Eros at number 2 Gosport Street was also his home, for around six months, in what was a cosy fisherman's cottage for the couple. It was here that he wrote a letter addressed to his American publisher, revealing his thoughts on Laugharne. He describes it as "a very odd town”. He wrote: "A good place, undiscovered by painters… because the sea is mostly mud and nobody knows when the water will come in or go out or where it comes from anyway.” The poet also famously described the town as “a timeless, mild, beguiling island of a town”. It was this walk that inspired the works of Poem In October, visitors can now walk in the very footsteps that led to him putting these famed words to paper.

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Description de la ville côtière de Laugharne dans le Carmarthenshire au pays de Galles, le long de l'estuaire de la rivière Taf, où a vécu le poète Dylan Thomas à partir de 1934. Lieux mentionnés liés au poète : Castle House sur Market Street (où il a rencontré Caitlin McNamara, appartenant à Richard Hughes), Eros au 2 Gosport Street (ancienne maison), et le Dylan Thomas Boathouse (occupé en 1949 grâce à Margaret Taylor).
